Marks of the Lord Jesus
MARKS uv thuh LORD JEE-zus
n. phr. (the scars of persecution Paul bore in his body, his answer to the circumcision party)
Greek ta stigmata tou kūriou Iēsou — stigma, a brand or mark pricked into the flesh, used of the marks branded on a slave to show whose he was; the plural gives the English word stigmata.

Definition · Webster 1828 · Scriptures · Corruption · Roots · Usage · Related

Biblical Definition

Galatians closes in Paul's own hand and ends with this: “From henceforth let no man trouble me: for I bear in my body the marks of the Lord Jesus.” The letter has been a sustained battle against men who were compelling Gentile believers to be circumcised so that they might glory in their flesh. Paul answers with marks of his own. The word is stigmata, the brand burned or pricked into a slave to show whose property he was, and his are the scars of the work — thrice beaten with rods, five times scourged, once stoned and left for dead, as he recounts to the Corinthians. His argument is therefore not a claim to superior spiritual experience but an appeal to ownership. These men boast in a mark made by a knife in a ceremony; Paul carries the brand of his Master got in His service, and that settles who he belongs to. The two verses before it set the terms: God forbid that I should glory, save in the cross of our Lord Jesus Christ. The marks are not the ground of his boasting; the cross is, and the marks are simply the evidence of a servant who has been where his Master sent him.

Webster 1828 Definition

Webster (1828): Mark, a visible line, impression or trace; a character or stamp impressed. Brand, a mark made by burning with a hot iron. I bear in my body the marks of the Lord Jesus, Galatians 6:17, the scars of persecution borne as a slave's brand.

expand to see more

Mark, a visible impression, line, or trace made upon a thing.

Brand, a mark made by burning with a hot iron, as upon a slave or beast.

Greek stigma (plural stigmata), a mark pricked or branded into the flesh.

Used of the brand identifying a slave's owner in the ancient world.

Set against those who would glory in the flesh, Galatians 6:13.

Key Scripture

Gal 6:17 — "From henceforth let no man trouble me: for I bear in my body the marks of the Lord Jesus."

Gal 6:14 — "But God forbid that I should glory, save in the cross of our Lord Jesus Christ, by whom the world is crucified unto me, and I unto the world."

2Co 11:25 — "Thrice was I beaten with rods, once was I stoned, thrice I suffered shipwreck, a night and a day I have been in the deep;"

2Co 4:10 — "Always bearing about in the body the dying of the Lord Jesus, that the life also of Jesus might be made manifest in our body."

Modern Corruption

The phrase was taken over to name the miraculous reproduction of Christ's wounds in medieval mystics, a sense wholly absent from Paul, whose marks were the scars of beatings.

expand to see more

The medieval and modern phenomenon called stigmata — the appearance of Christ's five wounds in the body of a mystic, reported of Francis of Assisi and others since — borrows its name from this verse and has nothing of its meaning. Paul's marks are enumerated elsewhere in his own hand and they are a catalogue of violence done to him by men: rods, scourges, stones, shipwreck, a night and a day in the deep. Nothing in Galatians suggests a miracle, and nothing in the New Testament commends the pursuit of visible wound-marks as a sign of nearness to Christ. Private revelations and bodily prodigies are not canonical evidence, whatever the sincerity of those who report them, and a devotion built on them has moved the ground of assurance from the cross to the believer's body.

A second and milder misuse turns the phrase into a boast of hardship generally, so that any wearying of ministry becomes a mark of the Lord Jesus. Paul's context is persecution for the gospel he had just defended, in a letter that refuses to glory in anything but the cross. The principle to recover is the slave-brand sense of the word. A servant's scars prove ownership, not merit; they close an argument about whose he is, and they are worn without self-pity by a man whose only boasting is in Christ crucified.

Greek & Hebrew Roots

Greek stigma, a brand pricked into a slave's flesh to mark his owner — Paul's scars of scourging and stoning, set against the circumcision party's glorying in the flesh.

expand to see more

Greek stigma (plural stigmata), a mark pricked or branded into the flesh.

Used of the brand identifying the owner of a slave or of cattle.

Greek bastazō, to bear or carry — ‘I bear in my body’.

Paul's own catalogue of the scars, 2 Corinthians 11:24-25.

Preceded by glorying in nothing save the cross, Galatians 6:14.
